planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or nursery starts out around the last frost in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this cultivar does not come reliably true from seed and is propagated vegetatively.

directions: Provence is a selected culinary thyme grown for its high proportion of thujanol in the essential oil, giving a rounder, fruitier, less medicinal flavor than ordinary common thyme, which is why it is prized specifically for herbes de Provence blends. It grows into a broader, more sprawling woody mound than upright French thyme, with wiry intertwining stems and small grey-green leaves. Shear back hard after the spring flowering flush and again in late summer to prevent the center from opening up and going woody, and replace plants every three to four years as vigor declines. Because it forms a wider mat than most culinary thymes, it also works well cascading over a raised bed edge or low wall.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species resents winter wet more than most creeping thymes.

directions: Native to the Azores, Madeira, and the northwest Iberian coast, this diminutive species forms a very low, dense tuft of narrow, spatula-shaped leaves that carry a resinous, almost pine-like fragrance distinct from the thymol scent of common thyme. In early summer it disappears under a haze of small bright-pink flowers that draw bees heavily. The tiny leaves can substitute for lemon thyme in the kitchen, but most gardeners grow it as a choice rock-garden or trough plant, where its compact tufted habit and unusual scent set it apart from sprawling creeping thyme cultivars. Give it gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or consistently damp ground, which quickly rots the crown.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively to keep the dark stem color and floriferous habit true.

directions: Herrenhausen is an RHS Award of Garden Merit selection distinguished from other ornamental oreganos by near-black stems and bracts that make the rose-pink flower clusters appear to glow, and by a tidy, non-flopping habit that holds up from June through the first hard frost. The young foliage emerges with a purple flush before settling to grey-green, adding a second season of interest before bloom. It is grown for pollinators and dried-flower structure rather than the kitchen, since its essential oil content is much lower than culinary Greek oregano. Cut the spent flower stems back hard in late winter to keep the woody base compact for another season.

subcategory: culinary herb bred for essential-oil content

planting.note: Transplant seedlings or rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; avoid rich, wet ground, which shortens the plant's life and dilutes flavor.

directions: Extrakta was selected as a commercial oil strain and carries a noticeably higher essential-oil content in its leaves than ordinary garden sage, translating into a bolder, more pungent flavor from the same amount of fresh or dried leaf. The narrow, upright green leaves are less broad than common culinary sage, and the plant sends up generous spikes of lilac-purple flowers in early to midsummer that draw bees well before most other kitchen herbs bloom. Because the flavor is more concentrated, cooks can use noticeably less of it per dish than standard sage, making it a good choice for drying and storage. Harvest leaves anytime through the season but cut for drying just before flowering, when oil content peaks.

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this form behaves exactly like common culinary sage in the garden.

directions: Albiflora is ordinary common sage in every respect except flower color: instead of the usual violet-blue spikes, it blooms in pure white in early summer, making it a useful choice for a white or moon garden where the typical purple sage flower would clash. The grey-green pebbled leaves are fully flavored and can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like standard culinary sage. It shares the same drought tolerance, sprawling woody habit, and need for excellent drainage as the species, and old plants benefit from a hard spring pruning to keep them from becoming leggy. Choose it when you want the culinary reliability of common sage without the purple flower color competing with nearby plantings.
